newsitem.title: UK: British bank results dominated by NatWest strategy.
newsitem.headline: British bank results dominated by NatWest strategy.

text.p: The British banks results season, which gets underway on Tuesday, will be dominated by an expected announcement on investment banking strategy at National Westminster Bank.
The fuss over NatWest will not entirely overshadow another generally good half for the established British banks and analysts expect profit levels to be translated into healthy dividend growth.
UBS banking analysts forecast an average dividend rise of 18 percent and that takes into account a rather meagre rise of eight percent at NatWest.

UBS sees the banks' dividend performance as a big highlight with aggregate headline profit growth of 15.4 percent looking rather flattering when compared to underlying growth of seven to eight percent.
Of the whole group and especially those banks with predominantly UK businesses, Lloyds TSB again looks the star performer.
It is expected to raise profits by around 30 percent to some 1.5 billion pounds ($2.5 billion) in the first half compared to 1.41 billion last year.
Lloyds TSB looks set to report a hefty fall in costs, unlike most others, and its high ratings are easily justified by the quality of its earnings stream, analysts say.

"Lloyds has been the best performer in the sector, its highly cash-generative business will ensure it soon accumulates enough cash to make other, value-enhancing, deals," said UBS analyst John Aitken.
In common with Lloyds TSB, Abbey National is expected to report some pressure on margins and only a modest mortgage growth.
Other areas, however are thought to have done well including insurance and consumer lending.

Abbey's first half profits are expected to have risen by over 20 percent to something like 675 million pounds but this comparison will be flattered by profits from its acquisition of the National & Provincial Building Society last year.
Of the major UK banks with large investment banking interests, NatWest is expected to dominate the headlines.

The bank has already said that profits will not be more than 770 million pounds in the first half due to the under-performance of its investment banking unit NatWest Markets which reported a net 77 million pounds loss on interest rate options.
Analysts will be looking for a clear statement from NatWest chief executive Derek Wanless who has temporarily taken command at NatWest Markets as to its future strategy.

Many would like to hear the name of Markets' new boss but this is thought unlikely. There has also been speculation that NatWest will remove the Treasury section from Markets and return to the UK bank.
This would make the investment bank unit easier to sell in the longer run if NatWest decides to go down that route.
In the figures, analysts will be looking hard at costs which are expected to be high given spending at NatWest Markets and the costs of restructuring the UK bank.
The other UK bank with major exposure to investment banking is Barclays which at the last full year stage took a concerted beating over poor results at its investment bank unit BZW.
BZW is expected to have done rather better in the first half than it did in a lacklustre second half of 1996.
In February, Barclays chief executive Martin Taylor warned that costs at BZW would continue at high levels in the first half with improvement in profit beginning to come through in the second half.
Elsewhere, margins are likely to be tight but the UK bank will benefit from the boom in consumer banking, analysts say.
Barclays headline profits are expected to decline slightly due to lower exceptional gains to around 1.23 to 1.24 billion pounds compared to 1.296 last year.
The final pair of banks are HSBC Holdings and Standard Chartered which have the majority of their business outside the UK.
Counted as the biggest banking group in the world by most measures, HSBC's profits are expected rise modestly to around or just below the 2.4 billion pounds mark in the first half.
HSBC and StanChart are the only two in the group to be affected by the strength of sterling and in HSBC's case the bank will also show lower exceptional gains.
At the operating level, however, growth is expected to be 10 percent or higher with its Hong Kong business doing well and its UK unit Midland Bank also contributing strongly.

Most of the Far East currency turmoil, mostly in Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines, has occurred since the end of the half-year but HSBC executives are sure to be asked about the effects of this for the rest of the year.
Standard Chartered's headline pre-tax profits are expected to have been more affected by a strong pound since it has very little UK revenue.
Forecasts range around the 440 to 450 million pounds mark after 448 million pounds last time.
Analysts see strong growth in StanChart's core Hong Kong and Malaysia markets but this will be offset by growing costs which the bank has already flagged. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
